claims.claim: Political ideology is a coherent set of beliefs and ideals about government and politics that helps shape political opinion and, eventually, policy.

The left–right political spectrum is a model for classifying ideologies along an axis; the left/right labels date to the French Revolution (1789), when delegates of the French National Assembly who upheld revolutionary values grouped themselves on the left and supporters of the monarchy on the right.

In the simplified standard form of the spectrum, the left generally prioritizes social, political, and economic equality, while the right prioritizes tradition, order, hierarchy, and limited government; moderates fall in the middle and try to balance the two extremes.
Classical liberalism is a political ideology based on belief in individual liberties and rights and the idea of free will, with little role for government.
Modern liberalism is a political ideology focused on equality that supports government intervention in society and the economy when it promotes equality.

Conservatism (modern conservatism) is a political ideology that prioritizes individual liberties and prefers a smaller government that stays out of the economy; conservative traditions also value established institutions and gradual change over rapid, untested innovation.

Socialism is a political and economic system in which government uses its authority to promote social and economic equality, providing everyone with basic services and equal opportunities and requiring citizens with more wealth to contribute more.

Libertarianism emphasizes individual rights and limited government intervention in private life and personal economic decisions; government's main function is to ensure domestic peace and national defense.

The single left–right line is a simplification: scholars and pollsters add dimensions or typologies to describe voters, and most Americans do not hold consistently liberal or conservative views (Pew 2014: the share of Americans expressing consistently conservative or consistently liberal opinions doubled over two decades, from 10% to 21%, while 39% took roughly equal numbers of liberal and conservative positions, down from about 49% in 1994 and 2004).

Ideology (a set of beliefs) is distinct from party identity (an individual's public attachment to a party — 'party identifiers'), although ideological thinking has become much more closely aligned with partisanship than in the past.

Political systems are not a clean either/or between 'socialism' and 'capitalism': OpenStax American Government 3e warns that treating the pair as a false dichotomy conflates partisan categories, and that real political systems, including the U.S., can possess aspects of both.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Can a single left–right line capture political differences, or is a multi-dimensional model needed?
positions: The one-axis left–right line is the dominant, standard way to describe ideologies, especially in Western countries (Britannica; OpenStax AG 3e presents it as 'one useful way').

The single axis is a simplification: political scientists add dimensions or create typologies to describe voter behavior, and Pew data show most Americans do not hold consistently liberal or conservative positions (Britannica; Pew 2014).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the line as a useful simplification, names its origin, and explicitly notes its limits using the Pew 2014 numbers and the OpenStax false-dichotomy warning.

positions: Classical liberalism: individual liberties and rights, free will, little role for government (OpenStax AG 3e).
Modern liberalism: equality-focused, supporting government intervention in society and the economy to promote equality (OpenStax AG 3e).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both meanings with attribution and notes that labels shift over time and place, so a label alone never settles what a person believes.

Facts synthesized into original prose; only the brief attributed working definitions are paraphrased closely.
